en: Majjhima Nikāya 69:
The Discourse to Goliyāni.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time a monk named Goliyāni, a forest-dweller who followed the practice of walking meditation, had come into the midst of the Saṅgha for some business or other.
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks concerning the monk Goliyāni:
“Friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha should be respectful and deferential toward his fellow celibate practitioners.

Friends, if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha is disrespectful and undeferential toward his fellow celibate practitioners, there will be those who say of him:
‘What is the use of this venerable forest-dweller’s solitary wandering at will in the forest, since he is disrespectful and undeferential toward his fellow celibate practitioners?’”
There will be those who speak against him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha should be respectful and deferential toward his fellow practitioners in the holy life.
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu, friends, who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, should be skilled in [the use of] seats:
‘Thus, I shall not sit encroaching upon the senior monks, nor shall I exclude the junior monks from their seats.
Friends, if a forest-dwelling monk who has entered the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha is not skilled regarding seats, there will be those who say of him:
‘What is the use of this venerable forest-dweller’s solitary wandering at will in the forest, since this venerable one is not skilled regarding seats?’”
There will be those who speak about him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha should be skilled regarding seats.
Friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha should also know the rules of proper conduct.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has gone to the Saṅgha and is living with the Saṅgha does not know even the rules of proper conduct, there will be those who speak of him:
“What is the use of this venerable forest-dweller living alone at his own will in the forest, since he does not even know the rules of proper conduct?”—
there will be those who speak of him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living with the Saṅgha should understand even the rules of proper conduct.
Friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living with the Saṅgha should not enter the village too early, nor should he return from it too late in the day.

If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living with the Saṅgha enters the village too early or returns from it too late in the day, there will be those who speak ill of him.
"But what [is the point] of this venerable forest-dweller living alone in the forest as he pleases, when this venerable one enters the village too early and returns too late?"—
such will be the critics of him. Therefore,
a bhikkhu who is a forest-dweller, having gone to the Saṅgha and dwelling with the Saṅgha, should not enter the village too early, nor should he return too late.
“Friends, when a forest-dwelling bhikkhu has come to the Saṅgha and is living with the Saṅgha, he should not go on a visit to families before or after the meal.
Friends, if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, having come to the Saṅgha and living with the Saṅgha, goes on a visit to families before or after the meal, there will be those who say of him:
‘Surely this venerable one, while living alone in the forest in his own way, has practiced wandering at improper times; that is why he behaves in this way even when he has come to the Saṅgha.’”
There will be those who speak against him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha should not go on a visit to families before or after the meal.
Friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha should be undisturbed and not fickle.
Friends, if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, having gone to the Saṅgha and living among the Saṅgha, is restless and fickle, there will be those who speak of him:

"Surely this restlessness and fickleness were cultivated by this venerable forest-dweller while he was dwelling alone in the forest at his own pleasure; that is why it now manifests even when he has come to the Saṅgha.
Thus will there be those who speak of him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha should be undisturbed and not fickle.
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu, friends, who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha should be not loquacious and should speak without incoherence.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha is loquacious and speaks incoherently, there will be those who would say of him:
"But what of this venerable forest-dweller who lives alone in the forest as he pleases, yet is talkative and loose-tongued?"—
such will be the critics of him. Therefore,
a bhikkhu who is a forest-dweller, when he has gone to the Saṅgha or is living in the Saṅgha, should not be talkative and should not be loose-tongued.
"Friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha should be easy to speak with and should have virtuous friends.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who has come to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha is difficult to speak with and has evil friends, there will be those who say of him:
'What is the use of this venerable forest-dweller living alone in the forest as he pleases, since he is so difficult to speak with and has such evil friends?'"
There will be those who speak against him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, when he has gone to the Saṅgha and is living in the Saṅgha, should be easy to speak with and should have virtuous friends.
Friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should keep the doors of his sense faculties guarded.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu does not guard the doors of his sense faculties, there will be those who speak of him:
"What is the use of this venerable forest-dweller living alone at will in the forest, since he does not guard the doors of his sense faculties?"—
thus there will be those who speak of him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should guard the doors of his sense faculties.
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu, friends, should be moderate in eating.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu is immoderate in eating, there will be those who would speak ill of him.
"But what of this venerable forest-dweller who dwells alone at will in the forest, yet is immoderate in food?"—
such will be the critics of him.
Therefore, a bhikkhu who is a forest-dweller should be moderate in food.
"Friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should be devoted to wakefulness.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu is not devoted to wakefulness, there will be those who say of him:
'But what is the use of this venerable one’s solitary dwelling in the forest at his own pleasure, since he is not devoted to wakefulness?'"
There will be those who speak against him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should be devoted to wakefulness;
a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, friends, should be one who has aroused energy.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu is lazy, there will be those who speak of him:
"What is the use of this venerable forest-dweller living alone at will in the forest, since he is lazy?"—
there will be those who speak of him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should be energetic.
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu, friends, should be established in mindfulness.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu is muddled in mindfulness, there will be those who speak of him.
"But what of this venerable forest-dweller who lives alone in the forest as he pleases, yet is one whose mindfulness is muddled?"—
such will be the critics of him.
Therefore, a bhikkhu who is a forest-dweller must be established in mindfulness.
"Friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should be concentrated.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu is unconcentrated, there will be those who speak of him:
'But what is the use of this venerable forest-dweller living alone at will in the forest, since he is unconcentrated?'"
There will be those who speak against him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu must be concentrated;
a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, friends, must be possessed of wisdom.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu is lacking in wisdom, there will be those who speak of him:
“What is the use of this venerable forest-dweller living alone at his own will in the forest, since he is lacking in wisdom?”—
thus will there be those who speak of him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should be wise.
Friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should apply himself to the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya.
For there are those, friends, who will question a forest-dwelling bhikkhu regarding the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, when questioned on the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya, does not manage to answer, there will be those who say of him:
"What is the use of this venerable forest-dweller living alone at his own pleasure in the forest, since he cannot answer when questioned on the Abhidhamma or the Abhivinaya?"—
there will be those who say this of him.
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should apply himself to the Abhidhamma and the Abhivinaya.
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu, friends, should apply himself to those peaceful liberations that transcend forms, the formless attainments.
Friends, there will be those who ask questions of a forest-dwelling bhikkhu regarding those peaceful liberations that transcend forms, the formless attainments.
"Friends, if a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, when questioned regarding those peaceful liberations that transcend forms— the formless attainments— is unable to answer, there will be those who say of him:
'But what is the use of this venerable forest-dweller living alone in the forest as he pleases, since he cannot answer when questioned regarding those peaceful liberations that transcend forms—
the formless attainments?'— thus will they speak of him."
Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should apply himself to those peaceful liberations, the formless states that transcend the realm of form.
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu, friends, should apply himself to superhuman states.
Friends, there will be those who ask a forest-dwelling bhikkhu questions concerning superhuman states.
If, friends, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, when questioned on a matter pertaining to superhuman states, does not succeed in answering, there will be those who say of him:
"But what is the use of this venerable forest-dweller living alone at his own will in the forest, since he does not know the purpose for which one has gone forth?"—
there will be those who say this of him.
“Therefore, a forest-dwelling bhikkhu should apply himself to the further states of human perfection.
When this was said, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, should these qualities be undertaken and practiced only by a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, or also by one who dwells in the vicinity of a village?”
“Friend Moggallāna, these qualities should be undertaken and practiced even by a bhikkhu who dwells in the forest, let alone by one who dwells in a village.
The ninth discourse, the Goliyāni Sutta, is finished.
